verses.text: Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to His disciples:
"The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' seat.
So practice and observe everything they tell you. But do not do what they do, for they do not practice what they preach.
They tie up heavy, burdensome loads and lay them on men's shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to lift a finger to move them.
All their deeds are done for men to see. They broaden their phylacteries and lengthen their tassels.
They love the places of honor at banquets, the chief seats in the synagogues,
the greetings in the marketplaces, and the title of 'Rabbi' by which they are addressed.
But you are not to be called 'Rabbi,' for you have one Teacher, and you are all brothers.
And do not call anyone on earth your father, for you have one Father, who is in heaven.
Nor are you to be called instructors, for you have one Instructor, the Christ.
The greatest among you shall be your servant.
For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You shut the kingdom of heaven in men's faces. You yourselves do not enter, nor will you let in those who wish to enter.
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You traverse land and sea to win a single convert, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of hell as you are.
Woe to you, blind guides! You say, 'If anyone swears by the temple, it means nothing; but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.'
You blind fools! Which is greater: the gold, or the temple that makes it sacred?
And you say, 'If anyone swears by the altar, it means nothing; but if anyone swears by the gift on it, he is bound by his oath.'
You blind men! Which is greater: the gift, or the altar that makes it sacred?
So then, he who swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it.
And he who swears by the temple swears by it and by the One who dwells in it.
And he who swears by heaven swears by God's throne and by the One who sits on it.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You pay tithes of mint, dill, and cumin. But you have disregarded the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness. You should have practiced the latter, without neglecting the former.
You blind guides! You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel.
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence.
Blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and dish, so that the outside may become clean as well.
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You are like whitewashed tombs, which look beautiful on the outside but on the inside are full of dead men's bones and every kind of impurity.
In the same way, on the outside you appear to be righteous, but on the inside you are full of hypocrisy and wickedness.
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You build tombs for the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous.
And you say, 'If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partners with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.'
So you testify against yourselves that you are the sons of those who murdered the prophets.
Fill up, then, the measure of the sin of your fathers.
You snakes! You brood of vipers! How will you escape the sentence of hell?
Because of this, I am sending you prophets and wise men and teachers. Some of them you will kill and crucify, and others you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town.
And so upon you will come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah, whom you murdered between the temple and the altar.
Truly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!
Look, your house is left to you desolate.
For I tell you that you will not see Me again until you say, 'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.'"

context.author: Matthew, writing to a Jewish audience
context.genre: Teaching discourse — a formal, escalating denunciation (the "seven woes") followed by a heartbroken lament, delivered in the temple courts.
context.audience: Both the crowds and Jesus' own disciples (v.1) hear this — a public warning about religious leadership, not a private aside.
context.setting: Almost certainly Tuesday of Passion Week, in the temple courts, immediately after Jesus has silenced every group that tried to trap Him in chapter 22. This is His last public teaching before the Olivet Discourse and His arrest.
context.custom: Phylacteries — small leather boxes containing Scripture passages, bound to the arm and forehead per Deuteronomy 6:4-9 — and tassels (tzitzit) worn on garment corners per Numbers 15:38 were genuine, commanded religious practices. Jesus' critique isn't the practices themselves but leaders enlarging them for visible display.
context.timelineImmediate: The last public confrontation before Jesus withdraws to the Mount of Olives for the Olivet Discourse in chapters 24-25 — this chapter closes His public teaching ministry in the temple entirely.
context.timelineBible: Jesus' reference to bloodshed "from Abel to Zechariah" (v.35) spans the entire Hebrew canon as it was ordered in His day — Abel's murder opens Genesis, and Zechariah's murder closes 2 Chronicles, making this a comprehensive charge covering the full sweep of Scripture's history of rejected prophets.

translation.meaning: Repeated seven times across the woes — originally "stage actors," describing a practiced gap between public performance and private reality.

occurrences.note: 17 of its 20 total New Testament uses are in Matthew alone.

translation.meaning: Those responsible for showing others the way while unable to see it themselves — a particularly sharp image for religious teachers.
The heavier, more substantial requirements of the law — justice, mercy, faithfulness — contrasted with minor tithing details some leaders over-focused on.
Tombs were painted white before Passover so pilgrims would visually avoid stepping on them and becoming ceremonially unclean — a beautiful surface hiding decay.

occurrences.note: Used only twice in the whole New Testament — here, and later when Paul himself calls a corrupt high priest "you whitewashed wall," echoing Jesus' own image.

gospelParallels.note: Luke's parallel set of woes against Pharisees and experts in the law, delivered at a dinner rather than in the temple.
Luke's version of the lament over Jerusalem, delivered earlier in his Gospel.
Mark's brief parallel warning about scribes seeking honor and status.

otBackground.note: The murder of Abel — the opening act of righteous bloodshed Jesus references in v.35.
The murder of Zechariah son of Jehoiada "between the temple and the altar" — the closing act of bloodshed Jesus references.
"Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord" — the words Jesus says Jerusalem will one day cry out, closing His lament in v.39.

context.sparkNotes: Jesus pronounces a series of woes against the scribes and Pharisees for valuing appearance over substance. "Whitewashed," describing their outward beauty hiding inward decay, is used only twice in the New Testament — Paul later borrows the same image against a corrupt high priest in Acts — and Jesus closes by quoting Psalm 118:26, the same verse the crowds shouted at His triumphal entry.

commentary.note: Henry reads the whole chapter as showing outward religion dressed up over inward rot — "the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees was like the ornaments of a grave, or dressing up a dead body, only for show." He notes the self-deceiving irony of v.30: they build monuments honoring prophets their own ancestors killed, never suspecting they're about to repeat the pattern.

JFB adds a vivid, timely detail: Jewish custom whitewashed tombs on a fixed day each year, specifically to make them more visible so pilgrims wouldn't accidentally touch one and become ceremonially unclean. Jesus was very likely speaking with freshly whitewashed tombs gleaming in plain view all around Him — not a random metaphor, but a picture drawn from what everyone could see that very day.

Gill unpacks 'mercy' as 'all acts of compassion to the distressed, relieving the necessitous, distributing to their wants' — precisely the practical, hands-on kindness he says the Pharisees 'very little practised, being a set of cruel, hard hearted, and covetous persons' beneath their meticulous tithing of garden herbs.
